country.comment: The desk review searched the 16 East and Southern African (ESA) countries covered by EQUINET and identified urban health equity initiatives in 12 countries listed in Table 1 (Angola, Botswana, Eswatini [also referred to as Swaziland on PDF pp. 3 and 13], Kenya, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe; with no information found for Democratic Republic of Congo, Lesotho, Mauritius, Namibia, plus Seychelles noted in Table 1). Ten detailed case studies were conducted in four cities across four of these countries: Harare (Zimbabwe), Kampala (Uganda), Lusaka (Zambia), and Nairobi (Kenya).

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative synthesis of desk-review documents and 10 structured case studies; no inferential statistical or numeric effect estimates are reported (only descriptive counts such as 30 pilot households in Epworth and 42 neighbourhoods / 56 micro-enterprises in Maputo).
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Across 52 desk-review documents and 10 case studies in Harare, Kampala, Lusaka, and Nairobi, participatory and recognitional equity mechanisms—including local participatory community-based targeting, community-led mapping, collective resident associations, multi-stakeholder co-design platforms, and community contracting—supported improved access to clean water, sanitation, drainage, and waste services in low-income and informal settlements (including a water-conserving toilet innovation introduced in 30 pilot households in Epworth and scaled via a local lending group, piped water and solar-powered boreholes leveraged by a residents' association in Hatcliffe, community-contracted slum water and sanitation infrastructure adopted into national Ministry guidelines in Uganda, and public sanitation/drainage hubs leading to a Special Planning Area and county MoU in Kibera, Nairobi). Conversely, provincial and district authorization requirements delayed WASH implementation in Epworth, while contested land lacking legal title, unaffordable municipal lease fees, weak formal planning links, and cumbersome local government operations impeded implementation and sustainability.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 5-11, Results (Tables 2 and 3); PDF pp. 11-15, Discussion (Table 4)

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 2 (mechanism directly observed empirically), respecting the design ceiling of 2 for qualitative studies appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist. Through 10 structured case studies drawing on 34 key informant interviews with direct implementers and 122 project/grey documents, the authors directly document concrete administrative, legal, tenure, and participatory mechanisms operating on water and sanitation interventions (e.g., provincial/district authorization delays and participatory targeting/water quality monitoring in Epworth, community contracting for slum WASH in Kampala integrated into national guidelines, Special Planning Area designation in Kibera, and collective association mobilization to secure piped water and boreholes despite lacking legal land title in Hatcliffe).
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 3, Methods; PDF pp. 6-11, Results and Table 3; PDF pp. 12-14, Table 4 and Discussion

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines informal/contested land lacking legal title and eviction risk (ELIGIBILITY: tenure), land-use/spatial planning gaps and Kibera's Special Planning Area (ELIGIBILITY: planning), unaffordable municipal land lease fees (BURDEN: fees), cumbersome county operations and provincial/district authorization requirements delaying WASH implementation (BURDEN: procedural_steps, delay), city councils waiving/sustaining leases despite non-payment, community contracting, and informal upgrading accommodations (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: accommodation), digital resident complaint/issue-reporting via Maputo's MOPA platform (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: complaint), extensive community participation, participatory mapping, targeting, and co-design (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: participation), and multi-stakeholder coordination across local councils, mayors, ministries, and NGOs (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: political_coordination).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, tenure, planning, fees, procedural_steps, delay, accommodation, complaint, participation, political_coordination
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 5-11, Results and Table 3; PDF pp. 12-15, Table 4 and Discussion

outcome_flags.comment: Water and sanitation access are directly examined in multiple case studies and desk-review examples (Epworth clean water and water-conserving toilets, Kampala informal settlement water and sanitation, Kibera rainwater harvesting and sanitation facilities, Hatcliffe piped water and solar boreholes). Service quality is examined via community and joint water quality testing/safe clean water in Epworth and quality sanitation in Lusaka. Administrative implementation delay is explicitly documented in Epworth where provincial and district authorization requirements delayed implementation of the water and sanitation initiative.
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 4, Tables 1 and 2; PDF pp. 6-10, Results and Table 3; PDF p. 12, Table 4

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Authors explicitly state on PDF p. 3 that they conducted a non-systematic 'focused narrative review, followed by structured case studies and content analysis' rather than a systematic review (ruling out AMSTAR 2), and collected primary qualitative empirical data via 10 structured city case studies incorporating 34 key informant interviews (with NYU IRB clearance and informed consent) alongside qualitative thematic content analysis of documents, with no primary quantitative analytical component (making CASP Qualitative Checklist the appropriate design-matched tool rather than MMAT).
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF pp. 2-4, Methods ('Sources of evidence' and 'Analysis of the evidence'); Figure 1, PDF p. 3

sample_size.comment: In the May 2022 desk review, 196 papers were identified and 52 documents (containing 64 initiative examples) were included. In June-July 2022, 10 structured case studies were conducted across 4 cities (Harare, 3; Kampala, 3; Lusaka, 1; Nairobi, 3), drawing on 122 published and grey literature documents and 34 key informant interviews. (Within individual case-study descriptions, specific initiative sizes such as 30 pilot households in Epworth and 42 neighbourhoods in Maputo are also mentioned.)
sample_size.value: 52 documents (64 initiative examples) in desk review; 10 case studies across 4 cities drawing on 122 published and grey literature documents and 34 key informant interviews
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 3, Methods ('Sources of evidence') and Figure 1; PDF p. 4, Tables 1 and 2

study_design.comment: Classified on PDF p. 1 as 'Policy and Practice Reviews' and operationalized in Methods (PDF pp. 2-5) as a qualitative multi-methods study: (1) a non-systematic focused narrative desk review of 52 post-2010 English-language documents across ESA countries, (2) 10 purposively selected structured case studies of sustained urban initiatives across 4 cities using 122 published/grey documents and 34 key informant interviews, and (3) manual thematic content analysis across 5 equity dimensions.
study_design.value: Qualitative multi-methods study combining a focused narrative document review, 10 structured city case studies (document review and key informant interviews), and manual thematic content analysis
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract and article type header; PDF pp. 2-5, Methods and Figure 1
